questions.q: In what order must legal entity, primary ledger, and business unit be configured, and why?
options: Business unit, ledger, legal entity — business units are always set up first
Legal entity, then primary ledger, then business unit — each references the one before it
All three can be configured in any order since they are independent objects
Primary ledger, then legal entity, then business unit
questions.explain: A primary ledger requires an existing legal entity, and a business unit requires an existing primary ledger, so the build order is legal entity, ledger, then business unit.

questions.q: What currency is assigned to LTV Canada Primary Ledger?
options: USD
CAD
A blended USD/CAD rate
No currency is assigned at the ledger level
questions.explain: LTV Canada Primary Ledger is configured in CAD, matching the Canadian subsidiary's statutory currency.

questions.q: What do LTV US Primary Ledger and LTV Canada Primary Ledger have in common by design?
options: The same currency
The same legal entity
The same chart of accounts structure and calendar
The same business unit
questions.explain: Both ledgers share one chart of accounts design and one calendar object, even though their currency and legal entity differ.

questions.q: What flag, set on both legal entities, allows the chart of accounts' intercompany restriction to work correctly later?
options: A flag marking the entity as tax-exempt
A flag enabling multi-currency revaluation
A flag enabling participation in intercompany transactions
A flag disabling Subledger Accounting
questions.explain: Flagging both legal entities for intercompany transaction participation is what makes the Company/Intercompany segment design in the chart of accounts function correctly.

questions.q: What should you verify before moving on from this lesson?
options: That every supplier has already been created
That both ledgers show a legal entity assigned, and both business units show a ledger assignment
That depreciation has already run for January
That the bank statement has already been loaded
questions.explain: A business unit with no ledger, or a ledger with no legal entity, silently blocks transaction entry later, so verifying these assignments now is cheaper than discovering the gap in Chapter 2.
